Superstore sales analysis: where the profit comes from, and where it leaks¶

Business question. A US retailer of furniture, office supplies and technology grew sales by roughly 15% a year between 2015 and 2018. Is that growth healthy, which parts of the business make or lose money, and what should management do in 2019?

What this notebook covers: data cleaning and validation, KPI analysis, seasonality, profitability by product and region, the cost of discounts, customer segmentation (RFM), and a back-tested sales forecast. Every chart in the charts/ folder is produced by this notebook.

About the data. Sample - Superstore is a widely used demonstration dataset (originally a Tableau sample): 9,994 order lines of a fictional US retailer, 2015-2018. The findings below are therefore a demonstration of method, not statements about a real company. The raw file used here also contains 806 empty rows, which makes it a realistic cleaning exercise. Source: leonism/sample-superstore. The notebook downloads it automatically if data/superstore.csv is missing.

Tools: Python, pandas, matplotlib, statsmodels.

In [1]:

2. Cleaning and validation¶

Rule: remove only what is provably wrong, log every step, and add assertions so the notebook fails loudly if the data ever breaks a business rule.

In [3]:
log = []
def step(name, before, after):
    log.append({"Step": name, "Rows before": before, "Rows after": after, "Removed": before - after})

df = raw.copy()

# 1) Rows where every business field is empty (only the IDs are filled in)
n = len(df); df = df.dropna(subset=["Sales"]);        step("Drop empty rows (no sales, customer or product data)", n, len(df))
# 2) Exact duplicates
n = len(df); df = df.drop_duplicates();               step("Drop exact duplicate rows", n, len(df))

# 3) Types
df["Order Date"] = pd.to_datetime(df["Order Date"], format="%m/%d/%Y")
df["Ship Date"]  = pd.to_datetime(df["Ship Date"],  format="%m/%d/%Y")
df["Quantity"]   = df["Quantity"].astype(int)
df["Postal Code"] = df["Postal Code"].apply(lambda v: f"{int(v):05d}" if pd.notna(v) else "Unknown")

# 4) Validation: fail loudly if the data breaks basic business rules
assert df["Row ID"].is_unique,                      "Row ID must be unique"
assert (df["Sales"] > 0).all(),                     "Sales must be positive"
assert (df["Quantity"] > 0).all(),                  "Quantity must be positive"
assert df["Discount"].between(0, 1).all(),          "Discount must be within 0-100%"
assert (df["Ship Date"] >= df["Order Date"]).all(), "Ship date cannot precede order date"

# 5) Derived columns
df["Year"]  = df["Order Date"].dt.year
df["Month"] = df["Order Date"].dt.month
df["Cost"]  = df["Sales"] - df["Profit"]
df["Ship Days"] = (df["Ship Date"] - df["Order Date"]).dt.days

print(f"Clean dataset: {len(df):,} order lines | {df['Order ID'].nunique():,} orders | "
      f"{df['Customer ID'].nunique():,} customers | {df['Order Date'].min():%Y-%m-%d} to {df['Order Date'].max():%Y-%m-%d}")
pd.DataFrame(log)

3. Business performance by year¶

Start with the basics: sales, profit, margin, orders, customers.

In [4]:
yearly = df.groupby("Year").agg(Sales=("Sales", "sum"), Profit=("Profit", "sum"),
                                Orders=("Order ID", "nunique"), Customers=("Customer ID", "nunique"))
yearly["Margin"] = yearly["Profit"] / yearly["Sales"]
yearly["Avg order value"] = yearly["Sales"] / yearly["Orders"]
yearly["Sales growth"] = yearly["Sales"].pct_change()
yearly["Profit growth"] = yearly["Profit"].pct_change()

total_sales, total_profit = df["Sales"].sum(), df["Profit"].sum()
print(f"Total sales ${total_sales:,.0f} | total profit ${total_profit:,.0f} | overall margin {total_profit/total_sales:.1%}")

def plot_yearly(ax):
    x = np.arange(len(yearly)); w = 0.38
    ax.bar(x - w/2, yearly["Sales"], w, color=TEAL, label="Sales")
    ax.bar(x + w/2, yearly["Profit"], w, color=SAND, label="Profit")
    ax.set_xticks(x, yearly.index.astype(str)); ax.yaxis.set_major_formatter(usd)
    ax2 = ax.twinx(); ax2.grid(False); ax2.spines["right"].set_visible(True); ax2.spines["right"].set_color("#CCCCCC")
    ax2.plot(x, yearly["Margin"], color=RED, marker="o", lw=2, label="Profit margin")
    ax2.set_ylim(0, 0.2); ax2.yaxis.set_major_formatter(PercentFormatter(1, decimals=0))
    for xi, m in zip(x, yearly["Margin"]): ax2.annotate(f"{m:.1%}", (xi, m), textcoords="offset points", xytext=(0, 7), ha="center", color=RED, fontsize=9,
                                                                       bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.15", fc="white", ec="none", alpha=0.85))
    h1, l1 = ax.get_legend_handles_labels(); h2, l2 = ax2.get_legend_handles_labels()
    ax.legend(h1 + h2, l1 + l2, loc="upper left", ncol=3, fontsize=8)
    ax.set_title("Sales, profit and margin by year")

Findings

  • Total sales $2.30M**, profit **$286k, overall margin 12.5%.
  • Sales grew from $484k (2015) to $733k (2018), about +15% a year, after a small dip in 2016 (-2.8%).
  • Growth came from more orders per customer (1.6 in 2015 to 2.4 in 2018, while customers grew only 16%), and each order got smaller (average order value $500 to $435).
  • Margin rose from 10.2% to 13.4% by 2017, then slipped to 12.7% in 2018: sales growth is no longer fully turning into profit.

4. Trend and seasonality¶

The seasonality index divides each month by the average month of its own year, so 1.0 means an average month and 1.85 means 85% above average.

In [5]:
monthly = df.set_index("Order Date")["Sales"].resample("MS").sum()
ma3 = monthly.rolling(3).mean()

# Seasonality index: a month's sales relative to the average month of its own year (1.0 = average)
tbl = monthly.to_frame("Sales"); tbl["Year"] = tbl.index.year; tbl["Month"] = tbl.index.month
tbl["Index"] = tbl["Sales"] / tbl.groupby("Year")["Sales"].transform("mean")
season = tbl.groupby("Month")["Index"].mean()
q4_share = (tbl.groupby("Year").apply(lambda g: g.loc[g["Month"] >= 9, "Sales"].sum() / g["Sales"].sum())).rename("Sep-Dec share of annual sales")
print("Strongest months:", ", ".join(f"{pd.Timestamp(2000, m, 1):%b} ({season[m]:.2f}x)" for m in season.sort_values(ascending=False).index[:4]))
print("Weakest months:  ", ", ".join(f"{pd.Timestamp(2000, m, 1):%b} ({season[m]:.2f}x)" for m in season.sort_values().index[:2]))
print(q4_share.map("{:.1%}".format).to_string())

def plot_monthly(ax):
    ax.plot(monthly.index, monthly.values, color=MID, lw=1.4, alpha=0.8, label="Monthly sales")
    ax.plot(ma3.index, ma3.values, color=TEAL, lw=2.6, label="3-month average")
    ax.yaxis.set_major_formatter(usd); ax.legend(loc="upper left", fontsize=8)
    ax.xaxis.set_major_locator(mdates.YearLocator()); ax.xaxis.set_major_formatter(mdates.DateFormatter("%Y"))
    ax.set_title("Monthly sales: growth with a strong year-end peak")

def plot_season(ax):
    colors = [SAND if v >= 1.25 else (MID if v >= 1 else GREY) for v in season.values]
    ax.bar([f"{pd.Timestamp(2000, m, 1):%b}" for m in season.index], season.values, color=colors)
    ax.axhline(1, color="#444444", lw=1, ls="--")
    ax.set_title("Seasonality index (1.0 = average month)")

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(13, 4.2), gridspec_kw={"width_ratios": [1.6, 1]})
plot_monthly(axes[0]); plot_season(axes[1]); save(fig, "02_monthly_and_seasonality"); plt.show()

Strongest months: Nov (1.85x), Dec (1.73x), Sep (1.64x), Mar (1.09x)
Weakest months:   Feb (0.30x), Jan (0.48x)
Year
2015    54.0%
2016    52.5%
2017    50.8%
2018    50.2%

Findings

  • Sales are strongly seasonal: November (1.85x), December (1.73x) and September (1.64x) are the peaks; February (0.30x) and January (0.48x) are the weakest.
  • September to December produce about 50-54% of each year's sales, so a stock-out or a weak campaign in autumn is very expensive.
  • The share of Sep-Dec sales is slowly falling (54.0% in 2015, 50.2% in 2018): the first half of the year is catching up.

5. Where does the profit come from?¶

Sales and profit by product group. The labels on the bars show the profit margin.

In [6]:
sub = (df.groupby(["Category", "Sub-Category"])
         .agg(Sales=("Sales", "sum"), Profit=("Profit", "sum"), Avg_discount=("Discount", "mean"))
         .assign(Margin=lambda d: d["Profit"] / d["Sales"]).reset_index())
cat = (df.groupby("Category").agg(Sales=("Sales", "sum"), Profit=("Profit", "sum"))
         .assign(Margin=lambda d: d["Profit"] / d["Sales"], Share_of_profit=lambda d: d["Profit"] / total_profit))
losers = sub[sub["Profit"] < 0].sort_values("Profit")
print(f"Loss-making sub-categories: {', '.join(losers['Sub-Category'])} | combined loss ${losers['Profit'].sum():,.0f}")

def plot_subcat(ax):
    s = sub.sort_values("Profit")
    ax.barh(s["Sub-Category"], s["Profit"], color=[RED if p < 0 else TEAL for p in s["Profit"]])
    for y, (p, m) in enumerate(zip(s["Profit"], s["Margin"])):
        ax.annotate(f"{m:.0%}", (p, y), xytext=(4 if p >= 0 else -4, 0), textcoords="offset points",
                    ha="left" if p >= 0 else "right", va="center", fontsize=8, color="#444444")
    ax.xaxis.set_major_formatter(usd); ax.axvline(0, color="#444444", lw=1); ax.margins(x=0.14)
    ax.set_title("Profit by sub-category (label = margin)"); ax.grid(axis="y", visible=False)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 5.4)); plot_subcat(ax); save(fig, "03_profit_by_subcategory"); plt.show()
cat.style.format({"Sales": "${:,.0f}", "Profit": "${:,.0f}", "Margin": "{:.1%}", "Share_of_profit": "{:.1%}"})

Findings

  • Technology (51%) and Office Supplies (43%) earn 94% of all profit, both at a healthy ~17% margin.
  • Furniture brings in 32% of sales but only 6% of profit (margin 2.5%).
  • Three sub-categories lose money: **Tables (-$17.7k, margin -8.6%), Bookcases (-$3.5k) and Supplies (-$1.2k)**. Tables brought in $207k of sales over the four years and still lost 8.6 cents on every dollar sold.

6. The cost of discounts¶

The furniture problem looks like a discount problem. This section tests that.

In [7]:
bands = pd.cut(df["Discount"], [-0.001, 0, 0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.5, 1.0], labels=["0%", "1-10%", "11-20%", "21-30%", "31-50%", ">50%"])
disc = (df.groupby(bands, observed=True).agg(Lines=("Sales", "size"), Sales=("Sales", "sum"), Profit=("Profit", "sum"))
          .assign(Margin=lambda d: d["Profit"] / d["Sales"], Share_of_sales=lambda d: d["Sales"] / total_sales))

heavy = df[df["Discount"] > 0.20]
loss_all = df.loc[df["Profit"] < 0, "Profit"].sum()
print(f"Order lines with discount > 20%: {len(heavy):,} ({len(heavy)/len(df):.1%} of lines, {heavy['Sales'].sum()/total_sales:.1%} of sales)")
print(f"Their profit: ${heavy['Profit'].sum():,.0f}  ->  they destroy {abs(heavy['Profit'].sum())/total_profit:.0%} of the total profit earned elsewhere")
print(f"Share of all losses (loss-making lines) that come from discount > 20%: {heavy.loc[heavy['Profit']<0,'Profit'].sum()/loss_all:.0%}")
print(f"Profit if those lines had merely broken even: ${total_profit - heavy['Profit'].sum():,.0f} ({-heavy['Profit'].sum()/total_profit:+.0%})  <- upper bound, assumes no lost volume")

def plot_discount(ax):
    ax.bar(disc.index.astype(str), disc["Margin"], color=[TEAL if m >= 0 else RED for m in disc["Margin"]])
    for i, (m, s) in enumerate(zip(disc["Margin"], disc["Share_of_sales"])):
        ax.annotate(f"{m:.0%}\n({s:.0%} of sales)", (i, m), textcoords="offset points", xytext=(0, 6 if m >= 0 else -26),
                    ha="center", fontsize=8, color="#333333")
    ax.axhline(0, color="#444444", lw=1); ax.yaxis.set_major_formatter(PercentFormatter(1, decimals=0))
    ax.set_ylim(-1.45, 0.42); ax.set_title("Profit margin by discount level"); ax.set_xlabel("Discount applied to the order line")

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4.4)); plot_discount(ax); save(fig, "04_margin_by_discount"); plt.show()

# Which sub-categories are discounted most?
sub["Share of lines >20% off"] = sub["Sub-Category"].map(df.groupby("Sub-Category").apply(lambda g: (g["Discount"] > 0.2).mean()))
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 5))
ax.scatter(sub["Avg_discount"], sub["Margin"], s=sub["Sales"] / 700, color=[RED if m < 0 else MID for m in sub["Margin"]], alpha=0.75, edgecolor="white")
offsets = {"Labels": (-6, 6, "right"), "Paper": (7, 3, "left"), "Envelopes": (7, -9, "left"), "Art": (-7, -11, "right"),
           "Accessories": (8, 5, "left"), "Furnishings": (-8, 7, "right"), "Phones": (11, -13, "left")}
for _, r in sub.iterrows():

ax.axhline(0, color="#444444", lw=1); ax.xaxis.set_major_formatter(PercentFormatter(1, decimals=0)); ax.yaxis.set_major_formatter(PercentFormatter(1, decimals=0))
ax.set_xlabel("Average discount"); ax.set_ylabel("Profit margin"); ax.set_title("Sub-categories with heavier discounts tend to earn less (bubble = sales)")
save(fig, "05_discount_vs_margin_subcategory"); plt.show()

  Lines Sales Profit Margin Share_of_sales
Discount          
0% 4,798 $1,087,908 $320,988 29.5% 47.4%
1-10% 94 $54,369 $9,029 16.6% 2.4%
11-20% 3,709 $792,153 $91,756 11.6% 34.5%
21-30% 227 $103,227 $-10,369 -10.0% 4.5%
31-50% 310 $195,315 $-48,448 -24.8% 8.5%
>50% 856 $64,229 $-76,559 -119.2% 2.8%

Findings

  • Order lines sold with no discount earn a 29.5% margin; at 11-20% off the margin is 11.6%; above 20% off, every band loses money (-10%, -25% and -119% for discounts above 50%).
  • Lines discounted more than 20% are 14% of all lines and 16% of sales, but they lose $135k. That equals 47% of all profit earned by the rest of the business, and 89% of all losses on loss-making lines come from them.
  • Across sub-categories the average discount and the margin move in opposite directions (correlation -0.52). Tables (26% average discount), Bookcases (21%) and Machines (31%) are the clearest cases.
  • Size of the prize: if the heavily discounted lines had merely broken even, profit would be $422k instead of $286k (+47%). This is an upper bound: it assumes no customers are lost when discounts are capped.

Caution: this is correlation, not proof of cause. Slow-moving or low-margin items may be discounted because they were already weak. A controlled pilot (see recommendations) would settle it.

Findings

  • 10 of 49 states lose money, together $98k. The worst are **Texas (-$25.7k), Ohio (-$17.0k), Pennsylvania (-$15.6k) and Illinois (-$12.6k)**; California and New York earn about $75k each.
  • The Central region has the lowest margin (7.9%) and the highest average discount (24.0%); West has 14.9% with 10.9% average discount.
  • Lines in loss-making states carry an average discount of 33.6%, against 4.2% elsewhere. The geographic problem is largely the discount problem again.

8. Customers: RFM segmentation¶

RFM scores every customer on Recency (days since last order), Frequency (number of orders) and Monetary value (total sales), each from 1 to 5, and groups customers by behaviour. Frequency uses fixed thresholds because many customers have the same order count; the segment rules are a judgement call and are shown in the code.

In [9]:
snapshot = df["Order Date"].max() + pd.Timedelta(days=1)
rfm = df.groupby("Customer ID").agg(Recency=("Order Date", lambda s: (snapshot - s.max()).days),
                                    Frequency=("Order ID", "nunique"), Monetary=("Sales", "sum"), Profit=("Profit", "sum"))
print("Orders per customer:", rfm["Frequency"].describe()[["min", "50%", "max"]].astype(int).to_dict())

# Scores 1-5: recency (lower days = better), frequency and monetary (higher = better)
rfm["R"] = pd.qcut(rfm["Recency"].rank(method="first"), 5, labels=[5, 4, 3, 2, 1]).astype(int)
rfm["F"] = pd.cut(rfm["Frequency"], [0, 3, 5, 7, 9, 100], labels=[1, 2, 3, 4, 5]).astype(int)
rfm["M"] = pd.qcut(rfm["Monetary"].rank(method="first"), 5, labels=[1, 2, 3, 4, 5]).astype(int)

rules = [(rfm["R"].ge(4) & rfm["F"].ge(4), "Champions"),
         (rfm["R"].ge(3) & rfm["F"].ge(3), "Loyal"),
         (rfm["R"].ge(4) & rfm["F"].le(2), "New / promising"),
         (rfm["R"].le(2) & rfm["F"].ge(3), "At risk"),
         (rfm["R"].le(2) & rfm["F"].le(2), "Lost / dormant")]
rfm["Segment"] = np.select([c for c, _ in rules], [n for _, n in rules], default="Needs attention")

order = ["Champions", "Loyal", "New / promising", "Needs attention", "At risk", "Lost / dormant"]
seg = (rfm.groupby("Segment").agg(Customers=("Monetary", "size"), Sales=("Monetary", "sum"), Profit=("Profit", "sum"),
                                  Avg_recency_days=("Recency", "mean"), Avg_orders=("Frequency", "mean"))
         .reindex(order).assign(Share_of_customers=lambda d: d["Customers"] / d["Customers"].sum(),
                                Share_of_sales=lambda d: d["Sales"] / d["Sales"].sum()))

# Concentration: how much of sales comes from the top 20% of customers?
cs = rfm["Monetary"].sort_values(ascending=False)
top20 = cs.head(int(len(cs) * 0.2)).sum() / cs.sum()
print(f"Top 20% of customers generate {top20:.0%} of sales")

seg_colors = {"Champions": TEAL, "Loyal": MID, "New / promising": "#8FBFB0", "Needs attention": GREY, "At risk": SAND, "Lost / dormant": RED}
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 4.2))
axes[0].bar(seg.index, seg["Customers"], color=[seg_colors[s] for s in seg.index]); axes[0].set_title("Customers per segment")
axes[1].bar(seg.index, seg["Share_of_sales"], color=[seg_colors[s] for s in seg.index]); axes[1].set_title("Share of total sales per segment")
axes[1].yaxis.set_major_formatter(PercentFormatter(1, decimals=0))
for a in axes: a.tick_params(axis="x", rotation=25)
save(fig, "07_rfm_segments"); plt.show()
seg.style.format({"Customers": "{:,}", "Sales": "${:,.0f}", "Profit": "${:,.0f}", "Avg_recency_days": "{:.0f}", "Avg_orders": "{:.1f}",
                  "Share_of_customers": "{:.1%}", "Share_of_sales": "{:.1%}"})

Findings

  • Champions and Loyal customers (41% of customers) generate 52% of sales. The top 20% of customers account for 48% of sales.
  • The "At risk" segment is the hidden opportunity: 136 customers who used to buy often (7.7 orders on average) but have not ordered for about 220 days. They hold $477k of sales (21%) and $78.9k of profit, more than the Champions ($70.8k).
  • 181 customers (23%) are dormant, with no order for about a year.

9. Forecasting 2019¶

Method: Holt-Winters exponential smoothing (trend plus yearly seasonality) on monthly sales. To avoid fooling ourselves, models are first trained on 2015-2017 only and judged on how well they predict the unseen 2018, against a naive baseline ("same month as last year"). The best model is then refitted on all four years.

In [10]:
train, test = monthly[:"2017-12-01"], monthly["2018-01-01":]

def fit_hw(y, seasonal):
    return ExponentialSmoothing(y, trend="add", damped_trend=True, seasonal=seasonal, seasonal_periods=12,
                                initialization_method="estimated").fit()

def metrics(actual, pred):
    return {"MAPE": float(np.mean(np.abs((actual - pred) / actual))), "MAE": float(np.mean(np.abs(actual - pred))),
            "Annual total error": float((pred.sum() - actual.sum()) / actual.sum())}

preds = {"Baseline: same month last year": pd.Series(train.values[-12:], index=test.index)}
for name, mode in [("Holt-Winters (additive seasonality)", "add"), ("Holt-Winters (multiplicative seasonality)", "mul")]:
    preds[name] = fit_hw(train, mode).forecast(12)
scores = pd.DataFrame({k: metrics(test, v) for k, v in preds.items()}).T
print("Hold-out test on 2018 (models trained on 2015-2017 only):")
display(scores.style.format({"MAPE": "{:.1%}", "MAE": "${:,.0f}", "Annual total error": "{:+.1%}"}))

best = scores.drop(index="Baseline: same month last year")["MAPE"].idxmin()
mode = "mul" if "multiplicative" in best else "add"
print(f"Selected model: {best}")

Hold-out test on 2018 (models trained on 2015-2017 only):

Baseline: same month last year 24.5% $15,468 -16.9%
Holt-Winters (additive seasonality) 18.5% $10,897 -9.1%
Holt-Winters (multiplicative seasonality) 23.0% $13,459 -19.2% 
Selected model: Holt-Winters (additive seasonality)
In [11]:
final = fit_hw(monthly, mode)
fc = final.forecast(12)
sim = final.simulate(12, repetitions=3000, error="add", anchor="end", random_state=42)
lo, hi = sim.quantile(0.10, axis=1), sim.quantile(0.90, axis=1)
lo.index = hi.index = fc.index
annual = sim.sum(axis=0)
y2018 = monthly["2018"].sum()
print(f"2018 actual sales:  ${y2018:,.0f}")
print(f"2019 forecast:      ${fc.sum():,.0f}  ({fc.sum()/y2018 - 1:+.1%} vs 2018)")
print(f"80% simulation range for 2019 total: ${annual.quantile(0.10):,.0f} to ${annual.quantile(0.90):,.0f}  (wide: only 4 years of history)")
scen = pd.DataFrame({"2019 sales": [y2018, y2018 * 1.10, fc.sum()], "vs 2018": [0.0, 0.10, fc.sum() / y2018 - 1]},
                    index=["Flat (no growth)", "Slower growth (+10%)", "Model forecast"])
display(scen.style.format({"2019 sales": "${:,.0f}", "vs 2018": "{:+.1%}"}))

def plot_forecast(ax):
    ax.plot(monthly.index, monthly.values, color=TEAL, lw=2, label="Actual")
    ax.plot(test.index, preds[best].values, color=SAND, lw=2, ls="--", label="2018 back-test")
    ax.plot(fc.index, fc.values, color=RED, lw=2.2, label="2019 forecast")
    ax.fill_between(fc.index, lo, hi, color=RED, alpha=0.15, label="80% interval")
    ax.yaxis.set_major_formatter(usd); ax.legend(loc="upper left", fontsize=8, ncol=2)
    ax.xaxis.set_major_locator(mdates.YearLocator()); ax.xaxis.set_major_formatter(mdates.DateFormatter("%Y"))
    ax.set_title("Sales forecast for 2019 (Holt-Winters)")

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 4.4)); plot_forecast(ax); save(fig, "08_sales_forecast"); plt.show()

2018 actual sales:  $733,215
2019 forecast:      $910,062  (+24.1% vs 2018)
80% simulation range for 2019 total: $588,042 to $1,230,146  (wide: only 4 years of history)
  2019 sales vs 2018
Flat (no growth) $733,215 +0.0%
Slower growth (+10%) $806,537 +10.0%
Model forecast $910,062 +24.1%

Findings

  • In the 2018 back-test the additive Holt-Winters model beat the naive baseline (MAPE 18.5% vs 24.5%) and under-forecast the annual total by 9%, so it is not systematically optimistic.
  • The 2019 forecast is about $910k (+24% on 2018). That assumes the 2016-2018 growth continues, so treat it as the optimistic end. The scenario table shows what flat and slower growth would mean.
  • The 80% simulation range is very wide (roughly $590k to $1.23M) because there are only four years of history. A monthly forecast with ~18% typical error is good for planning direction and seasonality, not for precise targets.

11. Recommendations and limitations¶

# Recommendation Evidence Expected effect
1 Cap discounts at 20% and require approval above it Lines >20% off lose $135k, 89% of all losses Up to +$135k profit (+47%) if no volume is lost; pilot first
2 Reprice or rethink Tables, Bookcases and Supplies (cost, supplier, minimum price) Combined loss $22k; Furniture margin 2.5% Moves Furniture from break-even to a contributor
3 Review discount policy in Central and in Texas, Ohio, Pennsylvania, Illinois 10 loss-making states, $98k lost; Central margin 7.9% Regional fix with the same logic as #1
4 Run a win-back campaign for the 136 "At risk" customers without deep discounts $477k sales and $78.9k profit sitting in a lapsed segment Even recovering a fraction is worth more than new acquisition
5 Plan stock, staff and ads around Sep-Dec (about half of annual sales); use Jan-Feb for low-cost retention rather than discounts Seasonality index 1.6-1.85x in Sep, Nov, Dec; 0.3-0.5x in Jan-Feb Fewer stock-outs at the peak; steadier cash flow

Suggested test for #1: cap discounts in one region for one quarter, keep another region unchanged, and compare profit and order volume.

Limitations

  • Demonstration dataset of a fictional retailer; no real business conclusions.
  • Four years of history; the forecast is validated on a single hold-out year.
  • Profit is taken as given. There is no cost breakdown, marketing spend or returns data, so causes of low margins are inferred, not proven.
  • Discount and margin are correlated; the causal link needs an experiment.
  • RFM thresholds are judgement-based and would be tuned with the business.
